title: Properties of Feedback
intro: A feedback amplifier trades open-loop gain for accuracy, bandwidth and controlled impedances.

blocks.text: An amplifier of gain A, with a fraction beta of its output subtracted from the input, has closed-loop gain

blocks.alt: Block diagram of a negative-feedback system. The input x enters a summing node, where the feedback signal is subtracted. The difference e goes into the amplifier A, whose output is y. The output is fed back through the block beta to the summing node.
blocks.caption: The standard feedback loop. The closed-loop gain is A/(1 + A*beta).

blocks.text: The quantity A*beta is the loop gain. If it is large, the closed-loop gain depends only on the feedback network (often resistors), not on the amplifier.
As A grows, the closed-loop gain flattens at 1/beta. The flat region is where the circuit is insensitive to A: a change in A from 1000 to 600 barely moves the output.

items: Gain desensitivity: dAf/Af = (dA/A) / (1 + A*beta). A 20 percent change in A produces a change in Af that is (1 + A*beta) times smaller.
Bandwidth extension: with a single-pole amplifier the closed-loop bandwidth is (1 + A0*beta) times larger, and the gain falls by the same factor. The gain-bandwidth product is conserved.

Impedance modification: series mixing at the input multiplies input impedance by (1 + A*beta); shunt mixing divides it. Voltage sensing at the output divides the output impedance by (1 + A*beta); current sensing multiplies it.
Linearity: nonlinearity is reduced by 1 + A*beta. Noise from the output stage is likewise suppressed but noise at the input is not.

blocks.text: Feedback reduces gain, costs a feedback network that loads the amplifier, and, above all, can cause instability if the loop gain's phase shift reaches 180 degrees where |A*beta| is at least 1. Stability is the subject of the next chapter.

blocks.title: Gain error
blocks.text: A = 1000 and beta = 0.1. Find Af and its error from the ideal 1/beta. Then find the change in Af if A drops by 20 percent to 800.
solution: Af = 1000 / (1 + 100) = 9.901. The ideal is 10, so the error is 1 percent.
At A = 800: Af = 800 / (1 + 80) = 9.877. The change is only 0.24 percent, compared with 20 percent in A (about 1/(1 + A*beta) = 1/101 of it).
blocks.answer: Af = 9.90 (1% below 10); a 20% drop in A changes Af by only 0.24%.

blocks.title: Bandwidth extension
blocks.text: An amplifier has A0 = 1000 and a pole at 10 kHz. Use beta = 0.1. Find the closed-loop gain and bandwidth.
solution: Loop gain at DC = 100, so the closed-loop gain is 1000/101 = 9.9.
The closed-loop pole is (1 + A0*beta) * 10 kHz = 101 * 10 kHz = 1.01 MHz.
Gain times bandwidth is about 10 MHz, the same as the original 1000 * 10 kHz.

blocks.title: Output resistance
blocks.text: A voltage-sampling amplifier has open-loop output resistance 1 kohm and loop gain A*beta = 100. What is Rout with feedback?
solution: Voltage sensing at the output divides Rout by (1 + A*beta): 1 kohm / 101 = 9.9 ohm.
